title: In Filtration 3
statementMd:
Maddy is still purging Baddy's evil army... for the third time!

The game takes place on an infinite Cartesian plane, which you may imagine as an infinite chessboard. Baddy controls n stationary **cannons**, placed at (x1,y1),(x2,y2),…,(xn,yn).

Under Chinese chess rules, a cannon attacks by jumping over a screen. If cannons A and B share a row or column and **exactly one** other cannon C lies between them, A attacks B (and B attacks A). Cannon C is their "screen."

At each step, Maddy may destroy a cannon **that is not currently attacked by any other cannon**. The destroyed cannon is immediately removed; it can no longer attack or serve as a screen.

Maddy wants to destroy all n cannons. Does there exist an order of destruction that clears the board?

## Input

The first line contains an integer T (1≤T≤105), the number of test cases.

The first line of each test case contains an integer n (1≤n≤2×105), the number of cannons.

Each of the next n lines contains two integers xi,yi (−109≤xi,yi≤109), the position of cannon i.

The sum of n over all test cases does not exceed 2×105. All cannon positions within a test case are distinct.

## Output

For each test case, output `YES` if some valid destruction order clears the board, or `NO` otherwise.

The answer is case-insensitive; for example, `yes`, `YES`, `Yes`, and `YeS` are all accepted as affirmative answers.

## Note

**Sample 1 Explanation**

In the first test case, the three cannons share a column. Initially, (0,0) and (0,2) attack each other over the screen at (0,1), while (0,1) is unattacked. Destroy (0,1) first. Then the other two are unattacked and may be destroyed in either order.

In the second test case, four cannons share a row. Initially, (0,0) and (2,0) attack each other over (1,0); (1,0) and (3,0) attack each other over (2,0). Thus every cannon is attacked, none can be destroyed, and the answer is `NO`.
